# PREFACE
## BY THE
### AUTHOR.

After I had decided upon this Work, and once I had formed its Plan, I hesitated a little on the Form I should give it. It was necessary to choose the one most likely to produce its effect in the world, and I balanced between the Method of saying nothing that was not a <term>Lemma<note>In mathematics and logic, a lemma is a preliminary proposition used to prove a larger theorem.</note></term>, <term>Proposition<note>A formal statement of a truth or a problem to be demonstrated.</note></term>, <term>Scholium<note>A marginal note or explanatory comment that clarifies a point in a mathematical demonstration.</note></term>, or <term>Corollary<note>An immediate consequence or conclusion that follows naturally from a proven statement.</note></term>, and that of mixing some Rhetoric with the Reasonings in places where it might be appropriate.

I soon settled on the latter, which appeared to me the most suitable for my aims. On one hand, People who know how to reason will follow me just as well in this manner as if I had restricted myself to pure Demonstrations; and on the other, the majority of Readers, who are intimidated by this Geometric Form, would have lost the fruit of a Work that I intend for them no less than for People versed in Mathematics.

The Design, which I propose for myself, is to examine, in the most exact and the

# PREFACE

...more thorough examination of the Resurrection of **JESUS CHRIST**, and to make this examination useful to everyone. I would never have achieved my goals if I had limited myself to reasoning only through <term>Lemmas<note>In logic and mathematics, a lemma is a preliminary statement used to help prove a larger point.</note></term> and other similar devices, the nature and usage of which are known only to very few people. By adhering even servilely to this Method, one loses many opportunities to push an argument further, to make it perceptible to all kinds of capacities, and to give it a power more capable of making an impression on the Mind than abstract <term>Theorems<note>A formal statement that has been proven to be true based on previously established statements.</note></term>.

One knows, moreover, that reasoning correctly and reasoning "in forms" <note>original: "raisonner dans les formes." This refers to the rigid, syllogistic structure used in traditional scholastic logic.</note> are two very different things, although they are not necessarily opposed. One can reason very correctly without doing so in Form, and sometimes the Form is observed even when one reasons quite poorly. An Oratorical Discourse may have such logical progression that, if stripped of its ornaments, it becomes nothing less than a rigorous demonstration; and the latter, in turn, loses none of its solidity by being adorned with all the flowers of the Oratorical Art.

Aiming to examine thoroughly the Resurrection of the Savior, which serves as the Proof and Foundation of the Christian Faith, I have done so with the same impartiality as if I did not believe it; I have acted as a perfectly disinterested person, who stands equal—

<meta>catchword: ly</meta> <note>The French catchword "ment" completes the word "également" (equally/likewise), which is translated here as "equally."</note>

constantly on my guard against the **Prejudices of the pro and the con**. Thus I have made no scruple of making the **Admissions** that appeared reasonable to me, and which in my opinion **Truth** required. For the same reason, I have nowhere intentionally suppressed the **Objections of the opposing Party**, when they were known, or when they seemed worthy of some attention on my part. When I reported them, it was without bad subtleties <note>original: "mauvaises finesses." This refers to deceptive or overly clever rhetorical tricks used to weaken an opponent's argument or make it seem less credible.</note>. I have neither concealed their strength to make them appear weaker, nor disguised the best of them to give them a false light, and to make them offensive. Avoiding with care everything that can be doubtful and subject to dispute, I made it my duty to always build upon certain Principles, and one will see that everything revolves around these two to which I have closely attached myself; one is the historical truth of the Facts, and the other is the Constitution and the Laws of Human Nature. Whatever consequences I have drawn from them, either for **Christians** or against **Deists** <note>Deists were 18th-century thinkers who believed in a creator based on reason but rejected organized religion and divine miracles like the Resurrection.</note>, I have done so, in the sincerity of my heart, only as far as the eternal Laws of Nature and Reason obliged me to do, and I have even carefully abstained from Conclusions that might appear forced.

If one does not wish to take my word for it, I appeal to my Book. Let it be deigned to be read

# P R E F A C E

<meta>catchword: He (translated from "Il")</meta>

*without prejudice, and I am certain that I will be given justice, and that one cannot condemn me without doing oneself more harm than to me. I feel no more inclination to give an unfaithful representation of things than I have an interest in closing my eyes to the Evidence when it is presented to me. I therefore ask for no favor. Let my Work be read, let it be weighed maturely; that is all I want, and if I fear anything, it is only Ignorance and hasty Judgments.*

*Whatever the case may be, I have some Reflections to offer to the Skeptics <note>original: "Incrédules." In the 18th-century context, this specifically refers to Enlightenment thinkers who doubted revealed religion or the possibility of miracles.</note>, into whose hands my Book may fall, and who perhaps also will read it with their usual Prejudices, and in a Spirit of Dispute <note>original: "Esprit de Dispute." This refers to a contentious attitude where one argues merely to win or to mock, rather than to find the truth.</note>.*

*I ask them therefore to observe that toward the end of Part III, where I summarize my Proofs, and where I draw my general Conclusion, I have added a Notice where I articulate all the possible means remaining for them to evade the force of my Reasoning, or to convince me of having reasoned poorly. This is so much trouble that I have saved them. They will see at a glance the various ways to attack me. They will only have to choose the best one. Is this not showing them an Example to follow? I sincerely seek only to settle <note>original: "vuider." An archaic spelling of "vider," meaning to empty, clear out, or settle a legal or intellectual dispute once and for all.</note> this important quarrel.*

It depends only on them for it to be promptly finished.

I have yet another Request <note>original: "Priere." In this context, it refers to a formal plea or petition to the reader.</note> to make of them, if they read my Book: it is to follow the thread of my Reasoning in itself, and not to raise objections based on certain Appendices that have no real bearing on the Matter. *In Part II they will find my Premises, and my Conclusion in Part III. If they can show that I state my position poorly, or that I conclude in the same way, I shall confess myself defeated. But, as I have never loved Dispute, which has for its object only small and frivolous quibbles <term>chicanes: the use of clever but misleading petty arguments to avoid the main point</term>, I will gladly leave to them all the glory and all the pleasure.*

Finally, if they have something to propose to me at any time, I expect them to do so in a clear, distinct, and precise manner. Let them not think to pay me in *arbitrary Reasonings*, in *Conjectures* plucked from thin air, in small strokes of *Criticism*, in *vague Comparisons*, or in *polished Thoughts*. I ask them to reason, and not to throw flowers at me <note>A metaphorical way of asking for substance over style; he wants logical arguments rather than mere rhetorical flourishes.</note>. Let them take every advantage; so be it; but let the *Digressions* <note>original: "Ecarts." Meaning deviations from the logical path or irrelevant side-tracks.</note> not be among them, and let one not try to substitute the brilliance of Wit for the solidity of Proof as soon as one feels its weakness.

# NOTICE
## FROM THE
### TRANSLATOR.

I have only two notices to provide. One is for all readers, and the other concerns only those persons who understand English and are familiar with the original work.

The former should pay attention to the brackets [ ] <note>original: "Crochets." These square brackets were a common typographical device in the 18th century to signal a translator's intervention.</note>, which are at the bottom of the pages; it is by these that I have distinguished the notes which are of my own making. I have not failed to do so anywhere, except in the Scriptural citations <term>Scriptural citations: References to specific passages or verses from the Bible.</term> which the author had entirely neglected. Thus, it is I, and not him, who must be held responsible if these citations are not always as accurate or as complete as they ought to be.

The other readers would be surprised if I said nothing of a small liberty I have permitted myself. I have split some sections in two; sometimes I have made only one out of two others; and in the second and third parts, I have introduced on my own authority a division into chapters. All of this seemed necessary to me to shed more clarity upon the discourse <note>original: "le Discours." Referring to the overall argument or treatise presented in the book.</note>. If, however, I have erred, the harm cannot be very great, since I have religiously bound myself to follow the subject matter in the manner that *Mr. Ditton* <note>Humphry Ditton (1675–1715) was an English mathematician and theologian. His work attempted to apply mathematical-style rigor to theological proofs.</note> presented it.

He also takes responsibility for adding the Scriptural citations that were missing in the original English version by Humphry Ditton.</summary>

### SECTION II.

*The particular Proof derived from the Resurrection of JESUS CHRIST is of such a nature that it ought to be neither despised nor ridiculed.*

Since the Proofs I have just indicated have been treated elsewhere by many Authors, and in a very extensive manner, I propose to examine another here, which will provide me with particular advantages in demonstrating that the Christian Revelation is divine. I refer to the *Resurrection* of JESUS CHRIST, who is the Author of this Religion.

This Resurrection is itself the great Article <note>In this context, "Article" refers to a fundamental point or formal statement of religious belief.</note> of Christian Doctrine. It serves as the foundation for everything else, and from it alone, in fact, one can conclude that all the rest is true.

Take this Article away from the Christian; he will surrender all the others to you without difficulty. Only this first one is important to him. It is here that all his present Consolation and his future Hope are founded, for both the Body and the Soul.

I know that the Deists <term>Deists: followers of an 18th-century philosophical movement who believed in a God of reason and nature but rejected the supernatural aspects of Christianity, such as miracles and divine revelation.</term>, with whom I am currently dealing, do not think this is so serious; their habit is to make light of it. ### SECTION V.

->*Nothing can excuse the indifference that the Unbeliever affects regarding the examination of this Historical Truth.*<-

I base the following **Corollary** <note>a logical consequence that follows naturally from an already proven statement</note> upon this. Since the **Unbeliever** runs such a great risk, in the event that the **Resurrection** of **JESUS CHRIST** is true, one of two things must be the case: either the **Unbeliever** possesses very clear and very convincing **Proofs** that this **Fact** is neither true nor probable; or the **Tranquility** he affects in the face of such uncertainty is not that of a prudent **Man**. Here is why: the peace he enjoys in this situation is anything but reasoned.

The **Tranquility** possessed by a prudent **Man** is a state of rest, an equanimity of soul, born of **Reflection** and resulting from a serious knowledge of the **Circumstances**. When everything is well balanced, and every comparison duly weighed, a **Man** finds nothing that leaves him with fear, sorrow, or remorse; that is what I call a **reasoned Tranquility**. Any peace of soul arising from any other cause deserves only the name of **mechanical Tranquility** <note>original: *Tranquillité machinale*; referring to a state of unthinking or reflexive calm that does not come from intellectual conviction or logic</note>, because it owes its existence either to ignorance

### SECTION XII.

What we have already said about it must have convinced everyone. ## SECTION XIII.

### *Proof of this wise relationship drawn from the Faith that is imposed upon us.*

Thus, whether the **Christian Revelation** be true or false, this Maxim of the Christians is always entirely evident: that **Obedience** and **good Works** are the certain consequences of a pure and real **Faith**.

### SECTION XXIV.

> *It is indeed impossible for the Deist to respect Natural Law as much as a Christian who is convinced of his Religion must do.*

THE Deist will therefore never have for the Law of Nature the respect that the Christian will render to it. Three considerations demonstrate the difference. 1. In the opinion of the Christian, this Law is an impression of the Finger of God <note>original: "Doigt de Dieu"; a common theological metaphor for divine action or authorship, referencing the tablets of the Ten Commandments.</note> who has engraved it in the heart of Man to lead and direct intelligent Creatures in a manner consistent with the Reason with which they are honored. Once it is recognized as divine, one cannot doubt that it deserves more attention, and that it has more influence on conduct, than it could have otherwise. 2. In the Christian System, the Promises and Threats, which constitute the Sanction <note>A "Sanction" is the mechanism—rewards or punishments—that gives a law its binding force.</note> of this Law of Nature, concern not only the present life but also the life to come. One sees how important this last Point is, since it must strike one more, beyond comparison, than all the present advantages or disadvantages that one might promise oneself from obedience, or that one might fear from Rebellion.

Let us compare the nature of these Crimes. If the **Resurrection of JESUS CHRIST** is false, Christians have rendered divine homage to an Object that did not deserve it. If the **Resurrection of JESUS CHRIST** is true, the <term>Deists <note>Deists were 18th-century thinkers who believed in a creator God based on reason but rejected supernatural revelation, miracles, and the divinity of Jesus.</note></term> have refused their Worship to the one they ought to have adored. Let us set Crime against Crime; that of the **Deists** is of a darkness that makes the Balance tip immediately. Let **Idolatry** be equal to **Blasphemy** in itself, if you will; but the affronts and the outrages that accompany the latter give it a rank—they make it an order of Crime—such that nothing similar can be imputed to **Christians**.

With all due respect to the **Deists**, we therefore believe ourselves fully entitled to maintain that the consequences of their **Error** must be incomparably more dangerous and fatal than those of our own.

### SECTION XXXVIII.

> *The present interest is so contrary to the Christian and so favorable to the Deist, that whichever of the two is in error, the Judge of the World will not treat them with equal severity.*

Let us make another reflection on this. If the Religion of J. C. <note>An abbreviation for Jesus Christ.</note> is false, it seems to me that a man who professes it in good faith gains nothing in this world; it even seems to me that he loses much in the way of Pleasures and Liberty. <term>Deism <note>The belief in a creator who does not intervene in the universe; popular in the 18th century as a "rational" alternative to organized religion.</note></term> is certainly on another footing. ### SECTION II.

From these two Propositions, I will consider myself justified in drawing my general Conclusion, which appears to me no less strong than it is clear. I will grant, if one wishes, that there is no Proof inferior to this one in its degree of Evidence <note>original: "Evidence" — in 18th-century logic, this refers to the self-evident clarity of a truth that the mind cannot reasonably deny.</note>, which is sufficient to merit a complete acquiescence, and which could be entitled to serve as law for a Creature endowed with Reason. Now, nothing less is required for that than solid and clear Proofs that withstand every kind of examination, and which no reasonable Objection can shake.

For what end, for example, can a Creature that we call rational have been made? I come now to my question. Here it is: *Was the first man created, or not, with the dispositions and the inclination to make use of his intellectual faculties <note>intellectual faculties: The inherent mental powers of reasoning, understanding, and judgment.</note> in proportion to the rational motives that would present themselves?* Let us propose the same thing in another way: *Did the first man receive, or did he not receive, from the Creator, a law engraved in his reason to determine the use he ought to make of it?*

If one answers no, I press the point, and I ask again: from where, then, did the principles and dispositions that served as a guide and rule for his reason come to the first man? From where did he derive them? If it was not from a natural impression, or if you will, from an innate law <note>innate law: The idea that certain moral principles or knowledge are present in the human mind from birth, rather than being learned through experience.</note>, we can absolutely conceive of only three other sources: *Tradition*, extraordinary *Infusion*, or the *Impression of Objects* upon the senses. Now, of these three means, the first was impossible; the second is contrary to divine wisdom; and the third is a true begging of the question <term>begging of the question: known in Latin as *petitio principii*, this is a logical fallacy where the argument assumes the truth of the conclusion it is trying to prove.</term>. This is what we shall see in the following three sections.

put into practice. Although God has given us Reason, He has not tied the essence of our Nature to the good use that we might make of it. By virtue of this *Liberty*, we can follow or neglect the duty that the adorable Author of our Existence had imposed upon us. That is to say, on one hand we can consult Reason and allow ourselves to be faithfully led by its voice, and on the other hand we can also either not reflect at all, or do so only with negligence—whether because we do not give ourselves the leisure to draw sound Conclusions, or because we despise, in practice, those that we have formed.

Regardless, it is the **natural Order**—and one that is never contradicted—that the Will only determines itself entirely based on some Conclusion, whether good or bad, clear or obscure. Otherwise, it would not be a **rational Faculty** *(a)*.

# RESISTANCE. Part. II.

Let us observe in this regard that the pleasure we take in yielding to **Self-Evidence** <term>Self-Evidence</term> <note>Original: "l'Evidence." Therefore, the Propositions can be so as well. Let us give an Example. This Maxim, *that Society could not subsist in the World if Men did not trust one another*; this Maxim, I say, is no less evident than the Axiom of Geometry which says, *that if to things equal to each other, you add, or subtract, equally, they will always remain equal*. Without understanding either Addition or Subtraction, everyone immediately conceives without difficulty that the whole of Society would be overturned if one had trust in no one.

Geometric Truths are demonstrated **a priori** <term>a priori: reasoning from self-evident principles or definitions that come before experience, often used in mathematics</term>, physical Truths **a posteriori** <term>a posteriori: reasoning based on observation and experimental evidence gathered from the world</term>, or by Experiments, and moral Truths derive their demonstration from Testimony, the Principles of Human Nature, and the Laws of the World. ## CHAPTER VIII.

*Showing the utility and necessity of admitting Moral Evidence in the affairs of life, and the terrible confusion that its rejection must cause.*

### SECTION I.

->*General plan for this Chapter.*<-

I have explained, in the preceding Propositions, the foundation, nature, and specific characteristics of **Moral Evidence** <note>The author uses "Moral Evidence" (Evidence morale) to describe certainty based on human testimony, authority, or historical records, distinguishing it from the "physical evidence" of the senses or "mathematical evidence" of logic.</note>, as much as seemed necessary for my subject. This was the first thing I had proposed to do.

The second task remaining for me concerns the utility and necessity of such Evidence. ### SECTION II.

*The danger of destroying Moral Evidence, in relation to the administration of Justice and the peace of States.*

I observe, first, that the entire administration of Justice—and consequently the preservation of the State—rests upon **Moral Evidence**. <note>As established in the previous section, "Moral Evidence" refers to certainty reached through human testimony and records, rather than direct physical observation or mathematical logic.</note>

## CHAPTER IX.

### *In which we show the absurdity & the iniquity of Pyrrhonism in matters of Moral Evidence.* <note>Pyrrhonism refers to an extreme form of skepticism. "Moral Evidence" in this 18th-century context refers to "Moral Certainty"—the kind of proof derived from human testimony and social experience which, while not as absolute as a mathematical proof, is considered sufficient for any reasonable person to act upon.</note>

### I. SECTION.

#### *General design of this Chapter, as well as the following one.*

After having established, sufficiently in my opinion, the nature & the utility of **Moral Evidence**, I shall offer some **Reflections** to show the **Spirit** of those who reject it, & I shall conclude with some others that might be useful for resolving certain difficulties, & for guiding Men in the search for **Truth**, in those Cases where this **Moral Evidence** is the only kind upon which one can rely. It is with this that I shall finish the second of the four general Headings that I had proposed, & I believe I shall have fully demonstrated that *the Proof as defined is of a nature that obliges all Men to accept it.*

### II. SECTION.

->*The different manner of spreading Pyrrhonism makes no real difference to it.*<- <note>Pyrrhonism refers to extreme skepticism—the philosophical position that one should suspend judgment on all matters because nothing can be known for certain.</note>

It is now evident that those who rail against **Moral Evidence** <note>In the 18th century, "Moral Evidence" or "Moral Certainty" referred to truths based on human testimony and experience, such as historical events, which are accepted as true by any reasonable person even if they cannot be proven with mathematical equations.</note> as being precarious, uncertain, and deceptive, do so only to mock the world, and that they are truly a great threat to the peace and happiness of the Public.

In this, I include all those who tend toward the same goal, regardless of the diversity of the paths they take.

There are some, I admit, who are at least estimable for their frankness. They proceed straightforwardly and do not wish to mislead us. Without further ceremony, they explain themselves in the crudest and most cavalier manner. They spare you the trouble of guessing their thoughts. These people tell you plainly that the *Proofs* being *alleged* to them are only good for *Fools* or for the *Pious*; that it is impossible to conclude anything certain from them; and that the only thing that is certain is that such and such things were said by certain people, whom one could bet even money were nothing but **Knaves** <term>Fourbes: A term for deceivers or "con-men" who use trickery to mislead the public.</term>.

### SECTION IX.

<margin>5. Advice.</margin> *Let your Conclusions faithfully correspond to the Principles upon which you have reasoned.*

When you have well and maturely weighed the circumstances, form your **Conclusion** according to the rules of the strictest **Logic**. Seek neither to dazzle nor to mislead yourself; and in this, as in all else, let **Reason** alone still be attentively consulted. Do you wish to know how to tell if you have done so? Are you yourself satisfied with your **good faith**? Does your **Conscience** not reproach you in this matter? When you reflect upon it with cool reflection <note>original: "de sang froid" — literally "in cold blood," meaning calmly and without the heat of passion.</note>, do you not feel a secret distrust regarding the manner in which you proceeded to your conclusion? If not, go, sleep in peace. Your **Conclusion** is solid, and you may rely upon it.

### SECTION XI.

7. **Advice.** *Where you cannot satisfy yourself, consult those who are skilled in this matter.* <note>original: "gens habiles" — referring to experts, scholars, or those with specialized experience.</note>

I have only one more piece of **Advice** to give for conducting oneself safely in the **search for Truth**; but it seems to me to be among the most necessary. It is that, if one cannot satisfy oneself through one's own efforts, one should feel no reluctance in consulting people who can be of assistance.

It can only be highly probable that persons who have devoted themselves to the study of a particular **Subject** must be capable of treating it more thoroughly and with more **Method**, than those who have never studied it, or who are applying themselves to it for the first time. Can it be shameful for anyone to take counsel from others on **Matters** that are of the highest importance? <note>original: "Affaires qui importent du tout" — essentially, matters that are of total or vital consequence.</note> Or can there be more shame in it than in consulting a **Physician** when one is ill?

### SECTION XII.

### *RESPONSES to the Objection made regarding the Difficulty of this Examination.*

#### I. RESPONSE. *We take just as much trouble for things of much less importance.*

But, perhaps someone will say to me, you are setting quite a task before us. <note>original: "voilà bien de la besogne que vous nous taillez" — literally "you are cutting out quite a lot of work for us," an idiom meaning to provide a daunting amount of labor.</note> How much time will it require? What pains will it not cost to put all these instructions into practice? The length and the difficulties of the Work frighten us far more than its importance encourages us.

I respond to this with three points. 1. Every day, men take much more trouble for Affairs that are of infinitely lighter importance. They rise early and go to bed late for a paltry profit, and all this without a murmur. If it is merely a matter of some Work that can make us valued in the World and grant us some reputation, the Mind exerts itself, subjects itself, and enslaves itself to everything without rest, and even often at the peril of health or life. Hardened to labor, tireless for such small Objects, why is it that the slightest difficulty discourages you, and seems insurmountable to you when it concerns the most essential matter of all?

If you say the latter, then, by your own admission, all the defects of **Human Nature** cannot serve as a reason for eternal doubt, and only prove the necessity of giving all one’s care, and of taking the greatest precautions to avoid **Error**. Now, do I preach anything other than that?

It may be that others have been mistaken in these researches, and that they have even fallen into very gross **Errors**. It may even be that this happened to them for having deferred to **moral Evidence** <term>Moral Evidence: In 18th-century philosophy, this refers to certainty based on probability, testimony, and experience, which—unlike mathematical proof—is technically fallible but practically reliable.</term>. But can the stone that made them stumble not be avoided by others, and will their fall be a reason for not attempting one’s duty? They have gone astray, you say, by counting too much on **moral Evidence**; well then; if this example biases you against it, what will you use? Do you believe that no false reasoning occurs in **Mathematics**, and has the abuse so many people make of the pleasures of life ever disgusted you with them? <note>The author uses a clever analogy: just as we do not give up on mathematics because people make mistakes in calculation, or give up on life's pleasures because some overindulge, we should not give up on seeking truth just because some fail to find it.</note>

# OF GOOD FAITH. PART II.

<meta>Volume I. Catchword: See- [Voi-]</meta>

...words, the most general Causes, and the most ordinary Sources of the **false reasoning** <note>original: "faux Raiſonnemens"</note> that one makes in the search for the **Truth**. One will see there that Men always contribute, in some way, to deceiving themselves.

1. They reason based on **Principles** that are not just, and from which, consequently, the Conclusion—though well drawn—leads them into **Error**.

One can be mistaken in this way by reasoning on Principles that are either too distant, or deficient in number, or exceeding in quantity. This last point, above all, is one of the most fertile in illusions. By dint of burdening itself with Objects, the Mind becomes muddled and confused. This causes one to draw Consequences that contradict each other, and in this embarrassment, one holds to the one that **Prejudices** <note>In the 18th century, "prejudices" typically referred to "preconceived notions"—judgments made before one has actually examined the evidence.</note> favor most.

2. Just as one can be mistaken by concluding correctly from false Principles, one is also mistaken in an opposite manner by positing well and concluding poorly. This commonly comes from **ignorance**, **inattention**, **haste** <term>Haste: In the original "précipitation," this refers to the intellectual error of rushing to a conclusion before the mind has clearly and distinctly perceived the evidence.</term>, **partiality**, and a thousand other things of the same nature.

Thus, sometimes one reasons on Principles that are not at all conclusive, and sometimes one draws false Conclusions from the most just Principles.

<summary>The author identifies two primary categories of logical error: starting with flawed premises (even if the logic is sound) and starting with sound premises but failing to draw the correct conclusion due to human failings like bias and haste.</summary>
<keywords>logic, false reasoning, principles, truth, error, prejudice, cognitive bias, epistemology</keywords>

## CHAPTER XI.

### III. *General Heading of the Plan of this Work, in which we establish the impossibility of God having invested Imposture with all the Marks of Truth.*

We pass to the third general Heading of the Plan we have formed. It consists in establishing the impossibility of **Providence** ever having willed, or permitted, that any **Imposture** should have all the **Marks of Evidence** <note>The "Marks of Evidence" (Caractères de l'Evidence) refers to the philosophical concept of "clarity and distinctness"—the criteria by which a statement is recognized as undeniably true.</note> that we have defined.

This needs no Proof for Persons who believe in the existence of a **Being**, such as must necessarily be the one who made and who governs the **World**. We shall therefore not burden ourselves with a useless task. Any Man who can know that **God** is eternal **Truth**, infinite **Goodness**, spotless **Justice**, and that He can neither mock His Creatures, nor give them useless **Faculties** <term>Faculties: In Enlightenment philosophy, these are the innate mental powers, such as reason, memory, and perception, given to humans by God.</term>—any Man, I say, who can know this, must understand, by simple **common-Sense**, that it is absolutely impossible for God to give to **Illusion** the **Marks of Truth**.

<summary>The author concludes a section on logical methodology and begins Chapter XI, arguing that a benevolent and just God would never allow a falsehood to appear perfectly and self-evidently true to human reason.</summary>
<keywords>Providence, Divine Justice, Truth vs. Illusion, Epistemology, Marks of Evidence, Rational Theology</keywords>

It remains only for me to draw a few **Consequences** from this **Principle**, and with that, I shall conclude my second **Part**.

1. ,, Wherever we surely find **Evidence** <note>original: "l'Evidence"; in 18th-century philosophy, this refers to "self-evidence" or the quality of a truth being so clear and distinct that the mind cannot doubt it.</note> as defined, we must give our **acquiescence** <note>original: "aquiescement"; the act of the will in accepting a proposition as true.</note> without fear of being mistaken.

2. ,, When **Events** do not correspond to what we had expected, it is because the **Proofs** upon which we reasoned did not sufficiently ground the **Conclusion** we drew from them. ,, It must be that we were mistaken in some place without perceiving it.

3. ,, When, by clear and incontestable marks, an **Imposture** is surely discovered, one must be certain that, if the **Proofs** used to make it believable were properly examined, they would appear frivolous and of the utmost weakness.

4. ,, When it comes to making believable those things that are of the utmost importance for the **Human Race**, we can be assured that **Providence** <note>Providence refers to God's proactive care and logical governance of the universe, ensuring that humans have the tools necessary for salvation and survival.</note> will cause them to be proposed with all the accompaniments of the **Evidence** required to oblige **rational Beings** to **acquiescence**.

I admit that this is not a direct **Consequence** of the general **Proposition**.

<vocab>**Evidence**: clear certainty; **acquiescence**: mental agreement; **Imposture**: religious or historical fraud; **Providence**: divine guidance; **Human Race**: all of humanity.</vocab>

However, it is one that follows immediately from the Proof of this Proposition—that is to say, from the infinite Perfections of the Supreme Being.

Indeed, divine Goodness <note>The author argues that God's benevolent nature ensures that humans are not left in the dark regarding their spiritual well-being.</note> is no less concerned with clothing important Truths with the degree of Evidence required to make them believable, than His other Perfections are concerned with not clothing Imposture <note>original: "l’Impoſture"; meaning a religious or historical deception presented as truth.</note> in such a way. I therefore boldly conclude that, with respect to all things concerning the salvation of Mankind, and which must have moral Evidence <note>In 18th-century logic, "moral evidence" refers to the type of certainty used for historical facts or human testimony, which is distinct from the absolute "mathematical" evidence of geometry.</note> as their Proof, we are sure, upon examining them, to find a degree of this Evidence proportional to the intrinsic value of these things, which will be sufficient, in every respect, to convince us of their reality.

We are now going to examine the Proofs of the Resurrection of our Lord **Jesus Christ**, in order to see whether or not they correspond to the nature of those we have just discussed. This is the fourth and final Article of the Plan that we had proposed for ourselves.

# GENERAL PLAN
<sig>A</sig>
<meta>catchword: con-</meta>

have all the characteristics of Evidence that indispensably compel the Mind to assent to them.

3. Finally, after having carefully examined the reasons that lead Christians to believe this Fact, and those that the <term>Deists</term> <note>Deists: In the 18th century, these were thinkers who believed in a creator God based on reason but rejected supernatural revelation, miracles, and the institutional Church.</note> allege for rejecting it, and having compared them with one another, we shall impartially weigh the Consequences of the faith of the former and of the incredulity of the others.

It is clear that by following this Method, based on the Principles we established in our Part II, it is absolutely necessary that we discover the weak point of either the Christian System or the Deist System. We shall infallibly encounter, in one or the other, those Conclusions so absurd, so contrary to sound Reason, which mark what is false in Logic and in the common practice of all Men of the world.

If it appears, in the Christian System, that one concludes the Resurrection of <term>J. C.</term> <note>Abbreviation for Jesus Christ.</note> against the Rules of Common Sense; that the Proofs alleged, when closely followed and thoroughly examined, are such that wise People can only regard them as frivolous, illusory, and non-conclusive; that the weakness of these Proofs does not stem from the inadvertence or the lack of skill of those who produce them—it being neither impossible that a good Cause be poorly defended, nor fair that it be...

### OF THE III. PART.

...condemned for this reason alone; but if the weakness of these Proofs stems from the very substance and nature of the things themselves; if this, I say, appears true of all of them in general, and of each one in particular, then the Dispute is over, and the Christian has lost. Indeed, it is impossible either that one should be reduced to an absurdity in defense of the Truth; or that God would oblige us to believe anything contrary to all the light of that **Reason** <note>In the 18th-century context, "Reason" was viewed as a divine gift—a "natural light"—that allowed humans to navigate the world and recognize basic truths, even if it could not fully grasp the supernatural.</note> which he has given us to discern the True from the False; although he may well require our faith in things for which Reason cannot resolve all the difficulties.

But also on the other hand, if the **Deist** <term>Deist</term> <note>Deists believed in a creator God but rejected organized religion and miracles, insisting that God does not intervene in the world after its creation.</note> can neither attack our view, nor defend his own, without arriving at Conclusions that are evidently contrary to **Common Sense**; if he is reduced to the necessity of resorting, to extricate himself, to Principles that are manifestly false and contradictory, or doubtful and precarious; if he cannot answer the difficulties except by subterfuge, or by diversions that cause the main Object to be lost from sight; in a word, if by reasoning methodically, he is forced to put forward things that serve only to entangle and obscure the matter, instead of giving a direct and precise Response to the Proofs alleged against him; then, I say, it is clear that the **Unbeliever** <note>original: "l'Incrédule"</note> does not have the Truth on his side, and that if he were...

### PLAN OF THE III. PART

...his duty, he would, without hesitation, grant the victory to the Christian.

All that remains for us to do, then, is to compare the arguments on both sides. It is certain that they must be as opposed to one another as are the opinions they establish, and consequently, they cannot both be equally true. It is necessary that on one side or the other there is *paralogism* <term>paralogism</term> <note>A piece of false or illogical reasoning, specifically one that the person making the argument is not aware of.</note> and *absurdity*; and consequently, it is enough to identify the party in which these are found to discover, in an infallible manner, the one that possesses the Truth.

It is not that the Christian might not have other proofs, beyond those provided by Reason, which convince him of the truth of his religion; but as these latter proofs are, in the Deist’s view, nothing but vain **enthusiasm** <note>In the 18th century, "enthusiasm" was often a derogatory term for religious fanaticism or the mistaken belief that one was receiving direct, private revelations from God.</note> or pure **chimera** <note>An illusion or a fabrication of the mind; something impossible or wildly fanciful.</note>, we must not even mention them here. It is to Reason alone that the unbeliever appeals, and it is to Reason alone that we must appeal against him.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "Testimonium Flavianum," the passage in Josephus’s works that mentions Jesus. ### CONCERNING ENEMIES.

of Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD), an early Christian scholar and theologian.</note>, that of *Tertullian* <note>Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD), a prolific early Christian author from Carthage.</note>, and that of so many others like them, who naturally should have taken advantage of such a precise Testimony, rendered by an Enemy and by a celebrated Historian, and who yet did not do so, regardless of whatever advantage might have come to them from it in their Disputes against the *Jews* and against the Pagans.

Here then are two opposing Proofs. On one side the affirmative Proof, and the negative Proof on the other. This latter provides, I admit, a powerful prejudice <note>In this historical context, "prejudice" refers to a strong preliminary reason for doubt or a pre-existing argument.</note> in many instances. It seems to me, however, that in the present case, it cannot be admitted against so many formal Depositions <note>Written testimonies or statements of evidence.</note>, and that one should give it all the less regard since one can give good reasons for the silence of these Writers, despite the authenticity of the Passage. I agree that if it is the interpolation <note>An entry or passage inserted into a text by a later hand, often implying a forgery.</note> of some Christian hand, the Fraud is most unworthy of a Christian, and must be all the more odious to the God of Truth. But I say that if the Passage is truly by *Josephus*, and if it was in the first Copies, one can easily reconcile that with the silence that the ancient Apologists <note>Early Christian defenders of the faith who wrote to explain or justify Christianity to the Roman authorities and the public.</note> kept regarding it.

If you ask me how? I answer that this could come from the Copies that fell into the hands of these Apologists, and in which this Passage was omitted.

It is not enough to sew in a Piece <note>Refers to the act of "interpolation," or adding unauthorized text into an existing manuscript.</note> opportunely; to set it in a suitable place; to adjust it so well that the Narrative is not disturbed; one must also capture the style and the air of the Author, and all of this seems to me a difficulty that few Interpolators <term>Interpolators: Scribes or editors who insert forged or external text into an original work.</term> can achieve without leaving some marks that betray the fraud. The thing, at least, is much more difficult to practice than it is to omit or cut out, in certain Copies, what one does not wish to be in the Author’s work. If, therefore, after a serious critical examination, one finds in the Passage regarding Jesus Christ <note>original: "J. C."</note> the style and turn of *Josephus*, it seems to me that its authenticity will no longer be doubtful to sensible persons, however plausible the Objections made against it may be.

# CONCERNING ENEMIES.

It is a fact known to everyone that the Ancients cited, as being by *Josephus* <note>The author refers to Titus Flavius Josephus, a first-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note>, several things that are found nowhere in his Works as we have them at present. Is it, however, believable that people who were writing for a Cause already very much despised and hated would have dared, in the face of the whole world, and in the midst of a thousand enlightened and learned Enemies, to falsely cite Authors known to everyone? If you grant these people even a modicum of shame or prudence—even if you were to believe them insensitive to the honor of their Religion—do you imagine that they could have had such audacity? What could they have to gain from it? Would not the slightest Adversary have easily discovered the imposture, and would this discovery not have branded the Falsifiers with eternal disgrace? Must it not have made them the laughingstock of their century and the contempt of posterity?

This is said without proof, and what is more, against all likelihood. For, as we have already stated, it is much easier to remove something from an Author than to add to one. If one replies, as certain people do, that Origen <note>An influential early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note> cited from memory, and could thus make *Joseph* <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> say what he had not read there at all, this is to mock people, and the evasion is pitiful. Is it then that the *Moderns* <note>The skeptical scholars of the author’s own time, the 17th and 18th centuries.</note> who treat the *Ancients* so cavalierly, have a privilege that the others did not possess? Do they never dream? And does it never happen that they cite falsely? But why must it be above all the *Christian* *Fathers* who are so often and so boldly accused of this weakness? The *Poets* and the *Historians* of *Paganism* are always excused. They are forgiven everything; even their faults become beauties. One never fails to find some mystery in them; they are admired; these are the "faults of *Praxiteles*" <note>Praxiteles was a famous ancient Greek sculptor; the author suggests that critics treat the errors of pagan writers as the masterful imperfections of a genius.</note>. In the Fathers, it is quite the opposite; nothing is excusable, and the greatest beauties are but false glitter, or <term>Fanaticism</term>, or <term>Enthusiasm</term> <note>In the 18th century, "Enthusiasm" often meant a dangerous, irrational religious delusion rather than simple excitement.</note>. ### TESTIMONIES

This is the spin he gives to things. JESUS CHRIST, according to him, performed only trifles, or rather he did nothing at all. How so? Was it nothing to restore sight and strength to persons who were entirely deprived of them? Everyone finds these to be great wonders; why then does this Prince <note>The Emperor Julian (reigned 361–363 AD), often called "the Apostate" by Christian writers because he rejected Christianity in favor of traditional Roman paganism.</note> speak of them with such disdain? It is because, by his account, several illustrious Pagans had done just as much, and that eyes and legs had cost them no more effort. JESUS CHRIST had therefore done nothing, because he had done no more than many others.

The reasoning is laughable, but in the end, does *Julian* deny the Facts? On the contrary, he posits them as true. It could certainly only be the force of truth that wrenched this admission from him, and does that not indicate that he had drawn these Facts from a source where he had also drawn others? The same means that taught him our Savior had healed the Blind and the Lame must also have taught him that this CHRIST raised men from the dead, and that he fed great multitudes with a provision of Food that would have hardly sufficed for ten people. I even dare to say that since the greatest Miracles of our Savior had the most Witnesses, they must have been more widely known than the others.

## SECTION IV.

### *The Forgery of Writings was also impossible while the Originals written by the hand of the Authors were preserved among the Christians.*

We may reason in the same manner regarding the period during which the Originals, written by the hand of the Apostles and Evangelists, remained among the Christians. As long as these Originals were available to be referred to and consulted, it was as if the writers themselves were still alive. I will not examine here exactly how long these venerable Writings were preserved in their Original form within the Christian Church. This discussion matters little to my subject, because I maintain only that it was impossible for anyone to succeed in substituting forgeries <note>The French "en supposer d'opposez" refers to the act of putting forward contradictory or fraudulent documents in place of the real ones.</note> while these Originals existed. ## SECTION V.

### *Forgery Could Not Subsequently Be Perpetrated by Any Single Party or Society of Christians.*

Independently of the physical Originals themselves, there is neither a Christian Sect nor a Christian Society that could have corrupted or forged <note>The original French uses "supposer," which in this context means to fraudulently substitute a false document for a real one.</note> the Writings of the New Testament in a manner that would have deceived all the rest. Opposing Parties watched one another mutually, and all together they shared the same interest in preventing Frauds that could have endangered their common Religion.

Whether punctuation is neglected; whether words are abbreviated; whether the person dictating uses a Copy that is poorly written or nearly erased; whether the resemblance of letters deceives him; whether he pronounces poorly while dictating; whether his eyes, dazzled by the same word repeated at some distance, make him omit what was in between <note>Scholars call this specific error "homoeoteleuton," where a scribe's eye skips from one word to a similar-looking word later in the text.</note>; or whether, for lack of judgment, he includes in the Text what a foreign hand had noted in the margin; whether the Copyist, for his part, does not hear the words dictated to him well, or his mind wanders; whether what he thinks, rather than what he hears, comes to the tip of his Pen; whether he yields too much to his own ideas; whether he knows little of Grammar, or does not understand ancient Spelling; these are all so many abundant sources of corruption in Manuscripts, and there is only too much to exercise the patience and the keen scent <note>original: "le nez," literally "the nose"—referring here to the critical intuition or discernment of scholars.</note> of Critics. consequence for the salvation of the **Human Race**. The Objection is plausible. It is striking, I admit, and yet I dare say that it is anything but well-founded in reason.

I agree that **Providence** is concerned with guaranteeing **Revelation** <term>Revelation: Divine truth revealed by God to humanity, specifically through scripture</term> from all stains which would render it unworthy of God and useless to Men. I consequently agree further that **Providence** must not have permitted this **Revelation** to be so disfigured that one could not recognize, with clarity, the divine will and our duty. That is the reasonable part of what the Objection supposes, and that is all. What more do those who make it demand?

Do they mean that God is obliged to perform new **Miracles** every day to achieve ends that his **Providence** can reach naturally, and through the ordinary ministry of Men? If that is their thought, the claim is unjust.

still in the world the greater part of *five hundred brothers who all at once saw* J. C. <note>original: "J. C." — abbreviation for Jesus Christ</note> one day after his resurrection.

Although, in an abstract sense, this great number of Witnesses is not in itself a convincing Proof of the truth of the Fact, it will not be denied that it is striking. An Imposture can remain a secret among a few people, but it could hardly be shared with so many without being exposed <note>original: "s'éventer" — literally "to get wind," an 18th-century idiom meaning a secret being leaked or discovered</note> in some way. One cannot, without extreme reluctance, accept the supposition that all these people could coordinate even the smallest details of a Lie; that they all deliver it with the same air of assurance; that all these False Witnesses agree so well in their depositions that they never contradict one another <note>original: "ne se coupent jamais" — literally "never cut each other off," a legal term for witnesses whose testimonies do not clash or invalidate one another</note>; and that they understand each other so perfectly as to deceive the rest of the world. Is this singularity not most surprising? In any other situation, a multitude of Accomplices is fatal to Plots, and you never see a Society of Rogues <note>original: "Fripons" — dishonest people or scoundrels</note> where there is not someone who betrays the others.

Let us not, however, dwell on these odious Comparisons, and say only that what gives a great degree of Probability to the Testimony rendered to the Resurrection of **JE-SUS-CHRIST** is that it was not rendered by one or two Witnesses only, but by a number much larger than has ever been <insert>seen elsewhere</insert>...

## SECTION IV.

### *The manner in which they frame their Testimony is equivalent to the most solemn Oaths.*

WHAT strikes one first and most forcefully is the manner in which they frame their Testimony. Nothing could be more august <note>original: "auguste" — meaning venerable, majestic, or inspiring deep respect</note>, or better suited to make an impression. They speak, they say, *(a)* only to obey God, with no other motives driving them. *(b)* They invoke that fearsome Name to implore His help and His blessings. They take Him as witness to their sincerity; *(c)* They propose their Religion as the Word and the Will of God, and say that *(d)* it is the only way by which they and their listeners can achieve salvation. In addition to the grave and heartfelt <note>original: "sensible" — in the 18th century, this meant full of feeling or emotionally moving rather than logical</note> manner in which all this is delivered, they boast of having received *(e)* from Heaven the power to perform Miracles to seal their Mission <note>A "Mission" refers to their divinely appointed task to spread the Gospel</note>, and what is more, they effectively perform these Miracles.

These Appeals to the Tribunal of God, these Invocations of His Name, which are made in such a public, frequent, and serious manner...

## VI. SECTION.

*They give their Testimony the greatest renown, and inform the world of it in the most solemn manner.*

To strengthen the preceding Reflection, let us observe that "the Witnesses of the Resurrection of JESUS CHRIST did not content themselves with speaking of it behind closed doors, and whispering it in the ear; they preached it as publicly as possible, and in the most numerous Assemblies."

This is not the secret of a <term>Cabal|A small, private group of people who plot together in secret</term>, or some muffled and mysterious rumor of a <term>Party|In this context, a sectarian group or faction</term>. The Apostles proclaim it with a loud voice in the Streets, and choose for this purpose a time when the City of *Jerusalem* was overflowing with Foreigners from all Nations <note>This likely refers to the Jewish festival of Pentecost, when pilgrims from across the Roman Empire gathered in Jerusalem</note>. The Crowd itself helped to awaken the Public’s attention. Everyone, without a doubt, was eager to hear the Witnesses, and the latter spared people the trouble of having to hunt them down. They went into the Synagogues; they presented themselves at the Temple; and everywhere they published the Resurrection of their Master.

But perhaps they only target the common people, and, counting on the gullibility of the masses, they would be the sort of people to lose their composure before enlightened listeners, and person-

What else could people do who felt themselves guilty, and who knew the Truth?

### IX. SECTION.

*One could not imagine the slightest worldly interest that they might have had in offering this Testimony.*

Here is another point of great weight regarding the Testimony of the Apostles, when considering it as a purely personal matter: "That they could absolutely have had no temporal interest <note>The term "temporal interest" refers to worldly or earthly gains, such as wealth, status, or political power, as opposed to spiritual rewards.</note> in preaching the Gospel."

Far from it; nothing could have been more contrary to their interests. For what could they expect from the world? What could they promise themselves but horrific consequences, enough to intimidate even the most resolute? It is therefore very evident, and with the clarity of a Demonstration, that these *Witnesses of the Resurrection* could not propose as the goal of their *Ministry* either *Esteem*, or *Riches*, or *Grandeur*, or the *Pleasures of this World*; and if they had nothing of that in view, what temporal *interest* could they have in it?

### SECTION X.

->*All the Prejudices of Birth & Education should have turned them away from this Ministry.*<-

IT IS another matter that deserves attention, that „ these Witnesses had „ all been raised in religious prejudices, very different from the Religion that they „ preached. 

They were all *Jews* by birth, and consequently, following the Prejudices of Education, they would not have been disposed to believe either that the Messiah had to die, or that he had to rise again. I am not speaking of the ideas that could be given by well-understood Oracles <note>In this context, "Oracles" refers to the Old Testament prophecies.</note>, and particularly the passages where *Isaiah* paints his humiliation and sufferings so vividly. I am considering the common opinion of the *Jews* who expected to see the Messiah come with pomp, to make them the most happy and flourishing People on Earth. The Disciples of JESUS CHRIST were certainly held by this Prejudice during his life, and, as they could not persuade themselves that he had to die, they had no less difficulty in convincing themselves of his Resurrection. Regardless of what those of their College <note>The "Apostolic College" refers to the original group of the twelve apostles.</note> who had [seen him] <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "seen" indicates the next page begins with this word.</note>

But when one considers that their entire mindset was to the disadvantage of the Cause they proclaimed; that their Education and their very Hearts had always been set against it, it seems that even the most demanding Judge should be satisfied. What Suspicions could possibly remain against the sincerity of these Witnesses? Here, there is no reason to fear the kind of superstitious stubbornness or credulous obedience that usually biases People toward the views of a National Tradition, especially one so deeply ingrained in domestic life.

But what am I saying? The path chosen by the Apostles was not merely contrary to the prejudices of childhood; it led toward the total subversion of the Religion in which they had been raised. I can express it this way in regards to the favorite opinion of the Jews: for them, Ritual was seen as the very essence of divine Worship <term>Culte (Worship): in this context, it refers to the formal system of religious practice and ceremony</term>, yet the Gospel was intended to establish a form of Worship very different from that of Moses.

# EXAMINATION
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

The two Religions could therefore neither coexist <note>original: "compatir" — used here in the archaic sense of being compatible or existing in harmony</note> nor subsist at the same time. The establishment of the one had to be the ruin of the other; and the Apostles, who were by no means ignorant of this when they bore witness to the Resurrection of JESUS CHRIST, must have been fully convinced of the truth of this Fact to deal such a mortal blow to the Religion of their Fathers.

## SECTION XI.

*If they had even a modicum of Conscience, neither the Religion in which they had been raised, nor that which they preached, would have allowed them to put forward such an Imposture.*

We have just seen that nothing less than a full Conviction was required to determine the Apostles to offer a Testimony so contrary to the Prejudices and so fatal to the Religion of their Childhood. Let us now observe that, "granting them even the slightest bit of Conscience, they could not bring themselves, in cold blood, to lend their Ministry <term>Ministry: in this context, it refers to their service or agency as messengers and teachers</term> to a Lie, because both Religions forbid, with the same rigor, every kind of fraud, and above all False Testimony."

# THE TESTIMONY
<meta>catchword: that it</meta>

The Integrity & the Virtue of the Witnesses is beyond dispute. They were neither people of intrigue, nor cunning, nor stupid, nor visionaries. They acted against all the Prejudices of their Childhood, & against all the reasons of their temporal interest. They were consistent with one another, & with themselves; Threats did not intimidate them, & Promises were unable to shake them. Their Procedure was frank & open, & Conviction alone made them follow [this path]. They indicated the Time, the Place, the Persons, & all the Circumstances to which one could recur <note>original: "recourir," meaning to go back to or consult for verification.</note>, if one did not wish to take them at their word. What they preached was not based on Hear-say. They spoke on the testimony of their own Senses, & as Spectators of what they announced. Finally, this Ministry made them lose the World, & left them no resource but in the expectation of another Life.

OF THE DEISTS.

## SECTION IV.

->*Two reasons which must ground this Objection, if it has any force; one is Certainty, and the other simple Suspicion.*<-

If the Objection raised against the Resurrection of Jesus Christ <note>original: "J. C."</note>, based on the fact that it did not happen in public, or that he did not subsequently show himself to everyone—if this Objection, I say, has any force, it must be for one of the following two reasons.

1. The Deists <note>Deists were 17th and 18th-century thinkers who believed in a God based on reason but rejected revelation, miracles, and the divine authority of the Bible.</note> present it as a formal and conclusive reason, or at least as a very just and legitimate Suspicion.

Or else 2. they seriously believe that it would have been, in all respects, more fitting for the conviction of Mankind, and consequently of more general utility, if Jesus Christ himself had personally given a Proof of his Resurrection that would have caused the same sensation <note>original: "éclat"; suggesting a public, brilliant, or striking display.</note> as his Death.

Whichever of the two it may be, we hope to show that one can conclude nothing reasonably from it against the Testimony of the first Preachers of the Gospel.

## SECTION V.

->*As for Certainty, it is far from being present, and the*<-
->*Suspicion is so vague that there is nothing reasonable*<-
->*to say to give it an air of probability.*<-

The OBJECTION cannot be given as a conclusive reason against the Resurrection of Jesus Christ <note>original: "J. C."</note>, because the conclusion in no way follows from the principles. *He did not show himself in public; therefore he did not rise. The Jews did not see him after his death; therefore his disciples did not see him.* This cannot be called reasoning, and the Deists <note>Deists were 17th and 18th-century thinkers who accepted the existence of a creator based on reason but rejected supernatural events like miracles or direct revelation.</note> would undoubtedly complain about us if we made them argue in such a manner.

For them, it all boils down to believing themselves legitimately justified in forming suspicions based on this. However, even these suspicions are not reasonable. For, even if we were unable to say why the Savior’s Resurrection did not have as many spectators as his death, it would nonetheless remain true that an All-Wise Being <note>original: "Etre tout-Sage"; referring to God’s providence.</note>, who sees things and judges them quite differently than we do, could have reasons for this that are unknown to us.

But, perhaps someone will say to me: here is God coming to your aid at every turn. He can do this, or he can will that; when you have not—

# CONCERNING THE DEISTS.

An indisputable proof that the Deists would not have yielded to the Evidence they themselves demand, is 2. that they reject all the Miracles performed by our Savior.

In whatever manner his Resurrection might have been attested, it is not believable that they would have yielded to it, since they do not yield to the attestation of his other Miracles; even though it is demonstrable that, if these latter had been nothing but trickery, the Christian Religion could never have made the slightest progress in the World.

They refuse to believe that **JESUS CHRIST** (a) went to many places in *Galilee*, teaching in the *Synagogues*, preaching there the *Kingdom of Heaven*, and healing all kinds of *Diseases*; that his reputation spread throughout all *Syria*, and into neighboring *Lands*, and that they brought to him *Sick People* of every kind, people afflicted with various ailments, those *Possessed*, *Lunatics*, *Paralytics*, and that he healed them; (b) that great *Multitudes* followed him, seeking to touch him, and that *Virtue* <note>In this context, "virtue" (from the Latin *virtus*) refers to a miraculous healing power or divine energy flowing from a person, rather than moral character.</note> coming out of him, he healed them all; (c) that the *Inhabitants* of a *Place*, having learned that he had come among them, they sent for him...

Here is the decisive point. Do we have Proofs, or do we not? Are the Proofs conclusive, or are they not? This point, once settled <note>original: "vuidé," an archaic legal term meaning to clear or resolve a case.</note>, decides everything. This is the knot of the matter, and it is to this that we must always return. If the Proof is sound according to all the rules, I shall not be astonished by a thousand difficulties people might raise—even if they were of such strength that one could not answer them—unless they lead to an impossibility or a palpable absurdity. If I am sure of the Fact, I have all I need. A few extra reasons would do no harm, I admit; but I can do without them, and with the certainty I have, I laugh at all the Objections that can be made.

We have finally demonstrated that if there are established Rules for distinguishing strong Objections from weak ones, all the Objections that the **Deists** <term>Deists: Philosophers of the 17th and 18th centuries who believed in a creator based on reason but rejected the supernatural elements of Christianity, such as miracles and revelation.</term> raise against the Resurrection of **JESUS CHRIST** carry no weight.

Now, I say that when all this is well weighed, the Proof we have of the Resurrection of **JESUS CHRIST** possesses every Characteristic of required **Evidence** <term>Evidence: In this context, "evidence" refers to "évidence morale," a philosophical term for a truth so certain that it would be unreasonable to doubt it, even if it cannot be proven by a mathematical formula.</term>.

## CHAPTER XII.

*Advice given to the Deists <note>Deists were 18th-century thinkers who believed in a creator God based on reason but rejected supernatural revelation, miracles, and the authority of the Church.</note> on the Method they are obliged to follow to refute this Demonstration of Fact <note>A "Demonstration of Fact" refers to a logical proof based on historical evidence rather than abstract theory.</note>.*

Before drawing my Conclusions from the great Result at which I have arrived, I have a Notice to give to the Deists; it is that, if they deign to reply to me, I expect from them something more than simple conjectures, or hazarded decisions. I have given them Reasons and Proofs; they must also give some to me.

If they wish to refute me, they have absolutely only one of two things to do: they have only to choose, and if they can do neither one nor the other, they will put themselves uselessly on the defensive.

1. *They must show that my Plan was poorly conceived, or that I have not fulfilled it; that the Principles <note>In this context, "Principles" refers to the foundational logical rules the author established in the second part of the book.</note> I have employed are foreign to the subject, and that they cannot serve the ends I proposed for myself.*

2. *If they grant me the Plan, they must show that its execution was poorly conducted,*

## VII. S E C T I O N.

*It is the same regarding all other sorrows, of whatever kind they may be.*

Another source of our sorrows on Earth is the dealings that bind us to the rest of Mankind. We lose our possessions or the people who are dear to us; we are subject to a thousand legal quibbles; <note>original: "chicanes"; refers to petty, malicious, or tricky legal harassment and disputes.</note> we must endure the weight of an unjust Power, the blows of backbiting, and the arrows of calumny. <note>The author makes a traditional distinction between "médisance" (speaking ill of someone, which might be true but is uncharitable) and "calomnie" (maliciously spreading false reports).</note> Let us not list every possible misfortune. Their number is too immense, and while all people are subject to them, it is known that the true <term>Faithful</term> <note>original: "Fidèle"; in this context, it refers to the devoted Christian believer</note> always bears the greatest share of them.

In this regard, everything contributes to our pains, and the present <term>constitution</term> <note>original: "Constitution"; here referring to the current physical and social order of the world as it exists in its fallen state.</note> of the world must naturally prepare us for them.

The **Body** is so weak that the slightest impression from the outside disturbs it. It takes almost nothing to cast it down, and the Principles of all Diseases, which we always carry within us, find only too many opportunities to break out.

We ourselves run toward the danger that we fear; we persist in our ruin, and often we have no greater **Enemies** than ourselves.

## XIII. SECTION.

->*Their opinion is thus equally contrary to Religion and to Nature.*<-

From all this I conclude that this **System** <term>original: *Systême*; likely referring to the controversial 17th-century doctrine of "Quietism" or "Pure Love," which suggested that a soul could reach a state of loving God without any desire for reward or fear of punishment</term>, whose nobility and spirituality are so highly praised under the pretext that it strips the love of **Duty** of all self-interest—this System, I say, is equally contrary to the **Gospel** and to **Nature**.

It is absolutely impractical as long as Men are Men. To turn it into a Law, one would have to remake **Human Nature** and make it something that it surely is not. Those who preach this system must either fail to study themselves at all, or, blinded by a false light, they persuade themselves—I know not how—that the love they have for themselves plays no part in the love they have for God. Whatever they may say, this is not the case; and if I am asked how they can be mistaken on this point, I would first point to the history of the world. There, one sees every day how false **Principles**, strong **Prejudices**, or the abuse of **Reason** and **Religion** can deceive Men, even regarding their own actions and thoughts.

## XIV. SECTION.

### *Furthermore, it is subject to terrible consequences for Morality.*

ONE will not accuse me of expressing myself in too strong a manner, if one considers finally that the **Dogma of entirely pure and disinterested Love** <note>original: *Dogme de l'Amour entierement pur & desintéreſſé*; This refers to the controversial Quietist doctrine suggesting that a soul should love God without any regard for its own salvation or eternal reward.</note> brings in its wake dangerous Consequences.

When, on one hand, you are given a Piety stripped of all Hope as the only true Devotion, and when, on the other, you are treated as unworthy, groveling, and as a sordid and mercenary Spirit, what can this result in for any Christian who cannot, in this regard, rid himself of natural human feelings? Does it not lead to a distaste for Duty, or at least a cooling of zeal for Religion?

I am willing to believe that the **Mystics** <note>Spiritual writers and practitioners, such as Fénelon or Madame Guyon, who emphasized internal prayer and the "disinterested" love of God.</note> have something else entirely in view. However, these Consequences are visible, and the proof of them is clear. In the weak and corrupt state of Man, we cannot have too many motives to lead us toward the love of God, and toward that of Duty.

This God, who made us, and who knows all our infirmities, from whatever side they— <note>The sentence ends abruptly due to the page break; the catchword "qu'el-" suggests the next page continues with "qu'elles viennent" (wherever they come from).</note>

To discover on which side the **Absurd** lies, let us delve deeper into the subject, and consider from every angle the Principle adopted by the **Deists**, *that one must resort to nothing other than Matter and Motion to account for everything called Reflection and Thought.*

## SECTION III.

### General plan for the *Examination* of this *System*, *following* the three *aspects* under which it is *fashionably presented* to better *conceal* its *mystery*.

To avoid trivial disputes <note>original: "la Chicane." In the 18th century, this referred to the use of legalistic tricks or petty arguments to avoid the heart of an issue.</note>, I begin with the definition of Terms, and I say that by the word *Matter*, I mean what all of Mankind generally understands—that is, *a solid Substance, capable of division, shape, and motion.*

I also give notice that in saying that the Deists <note>The author uses "Deists" here as a broad label for materialist thinkers who argued that the universe and the human mind could be explained entirely through physical laws without needing a separate spiritual soul.</note> claim to explain all the *Phenomena* of *Thought* by the *motion* of *Matter*, my intention is not that this must be understood to the exclusion of all other properties of this *Matter*. *Matter.* To speak of its properties is to speak also of their combinations, since all of these combinations, however one might imagine them, ultimately boil down to shape and motion.

<header>S U P P L E M E N T. 293</header>

If these Laws of Matter invincibly oppose the production of that which bears the name of *Reasoning*, *Reflection*, *Volition* <note>The faculty of willing or choosing.</note>, and other similar things, it is demonstrably evident that these things cannot be the result of any of these Qualities of Matter. For there is no Effect that can be produced by a Cause that is repugnant to it, and which is incompatible with it by constant and certain Laws.

Here then, in a word, is what we have to demonstrate: that the *Actions or operations of thinking Beings are entirely incompatible with the Laws of Matter, and its known Properties, which are solidity, figure* <note>The physical shape or geometric form of an object.</note>, *divisibility, and motion.*

This is the Demonstration that we are going to provide in the *Propositions* that follow.

Once this Principle <note>Referring to the principle on page 294: that identical physical causes must produce identical physical effects, which contradicts the diversity of thought.</note> is established, the Proof of my Proposition is easy. When I conclude *from one thing to another*, I clearly perceive, in the Reasoning <term>Reasoning (Raisonnement): The logical process of moving from known facts to a new conclusion.</term> that I perform, *two manners*, or two distinct species of thinking. The Names one might wish to give them matter little to me, provided that a real difference in these Operations of the Mind is granted to me. One of these manners of thinking consists in the Acquiescence <term>Acquiescence (Aquiescement): Here meaning "mental assent" or the internal recognition that a statement is true.</term> that I give to the truth of the Propositions, which are commonly called the *Premises*. By the other, I acquiesce to the truth of a certain Proposition which results from the preceding ones, and which is called the *Conclusion*; so that this latter becomes the object of my Acquiescence as a consequence of the relation and the connection that I discover between it and those Premises which, before concluding anything from them, had already appeared to me as entirely reasonable.

These two Operations of the Mind, of which one acquiesces to the Premises and the other to the Conclusion, are evidently of an entirely different species or nature; because, in the *Conclusion*, I perceive the agreement that two things have between them by means of the prior agreement I discover between these two things and a third, which is not actually in the Conclusion, even if it were in the two <note>The text cuts off here; the author is describing a syllogism, where a "middle term" links two ideas in the premises but disappears in the final conclusion.</note>

###

It matters little to me what Names one might wish to give them, provided that a real difference is granted in these Operations of the Mind <term>Operations of the Mind (Operations de l'Esprit): A classical philosophical term for the different functions of the intellect, such as perception, judgment, and the act of reasoning.</term>. By the other, I acquiesce to the truth of a certain Proposition which results from the preceding ones, and which is called the *Conclusion*; so that this latter becomes the object of my Acquiescence as a consequence of the relation and the connection that I discover between it and those Premises which, before concluding anything from them, had already appeared entirely reasonable to me.

These two Operations of the Mind—one of which acquiesces to the Premises, and the other to the Conclusion—are evidently of an entirely different species or nature; because, in the *Conclusion*, I perceive the agreement that two things have between them by means of the prior agreement I discover between these two things and a third <note>This refers to the "middle term" in a syllogism, the logical bridge that connects the subject and predicate of a conclusion.</note>, which is not actually in the Conclusion, even though it may have been in the two...
