If Matter has the power of Movement by itself, it must be either in one particular direction <term>determination: in 18th-century physics, this refers to the specific direction or path an object takes</term>, or in all *possible directions*; or in the directions that it *judges to be the most appropriate according to the requirements of the Case*.

As for the second, it appears that the power to give oneself all possible directions places Matter in a state of indeterminacy and absolute indifference <note>Indifference here refers to a state where there is no specific reason or "motive" for a material body to choose one direction over another, resulting in a lack of action.</note>. This is to strip it of all faculty to move itself, because the power to move in every direction is the power to move in none—that is, not to move at all. Thus, this other Supposition is a manifest contradiction.

For he was a great Disputer, and excessively stubborn, unable to suffer either the people who asked him for clarifications, or those who contradicted him, and even carrying his heat into Dispute to the point of anger until the end of his life, according to what the same *A. Wood* says in the Article on Hobbes, and in that of *Glanvill.* <note>Joseph Glanvill (1636–1680), an English philosopher and clergyman who was often in intellectual conflict with Hobbes's views.</note>

But what convinces me more than anything else of the falseness of this System is that, by following the ideas of *Hobbes* <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) was an English philosopher who proposed that all human thought and sensation are merely physical movements of matter within the body.</note>, it is impossible for the Perception of Objects to maintain the specific difference <note>In philosophy, a "specific difference" is the essential quality that distinguishes one species or category from another.</note> between them that Nature has established. For if Perception is nothing other than the resistance or the repercussion <note>A term used here to mean "reaction" or the physical act of pushing back.</note> of the Organ, it is evident that the difference between Sensations arises only from the diversity in the resistance of the Sense Organ, and that consequently the former differ from one another only in proportion and in the same respects that the latter admits differences.

Now, in considering these differences in relation to the resistance of the Sense Organ, there can only be the following:

1. The Repercussion is more or less strong, depending on whether the impact coming from the Object has more or less force.

2. More or fewer parts of the Organ resist, according to whether there are more or fewer of them—both in quantity and in extent—that receive the impression of the Object.

3. Finally, the difference can come from the position and the situation of the parts, so that sometimes these, and sometimes those, are put into a state of resistance according to the form and the figure of the presented Object.

Let us see distinctly what can result from each of these.

## SECTION V.

# S U P P L E M E N T.

Let them produce only a few reasons that might make it <note>Referring to the theory of a "Common Soul" animating all things.</note> probable.

In the meantime, I shall provide them with one that will make its improbability more than probable.

It will no doubt be granted to me that men are not *Automata* <note>Self-operating machines; in 18th-century philosophy, this often referred to the idea of bodies functioning without an individual soul.</note> for whom the *World Soul* <note>original: *Ame du Monde* — the ancient concept, often associated with Neoplatonism, that a single spirit animates the entire universe.</note> serves as a *Common Form*. *Thought* and *Reflection* prove to us, by *internal feeling* <note>original: *sentiment intérieur* — the direct, private awareness or "common sense" one has of their own existence and mental states.</note>, that there is in us some *Principle* other than *Matter*, and which is the sole *Agent* that thinks and reflects.

This being established, I say that our *Thoughts* and our *Reflections* cannot have, in each of us, a *Common Intelligence* for their agent; since we do not know at all, by *internal feeling*, what is happening in the *Mind* of others.

I should very much like to be told how and why this *Soul*, which is supposed to be universal, would be ignorant in one *Body* of what it does in another? It is itself, and it alone, which thinks here, there, and everywhere. The *Thought* of this man, that of a second, that of a third, that of everyone, is but one *common Soul* which thinks and reflects at the same time in all these various portions of *Matter*. ## IX. S E C T I O N.

->*The reasons proving the immateriality*<-
->*of our Soul also prove that it does*<-

Whatever may be the case regarding what becomes of the **Soul of Beasts** <note>original: "l'Ame des Brutes." In early modern philosophy, "brutes" was the standard term for animals, used to distinguish them from humans, who were considered "rational souls."</note> upon the dissolution of their **Bodies**, we can boldly affirm of our own what we established in the fourth **Consequence** of **Section VII** of this **Supplement**. This refers to the human being viewed as a combination of two distinct things: a physical body and a spiritual soul.</note> they had animated.

If, in the nature of things, the **thinking Substance** is intrinsically and essentially distinct from **Matter**, and if consequently it is not at all susceptible to the same **vicissitudes** <note>Changes or shifts in state; here referring specifically to the physical decay and breakdown that affects material objects.</note>, it is not only *possible*, but also *very probable* and *very apparent*, that the former continues to be and to act after the latter has ceased to be a suitable dwelling place for it.

On how many occasions does it not appear to us the height of impertinence to build **Systems** <note>Theories or philosophical frameworks.</note> upon the **absolute Power of God**, while His **Will** is entirely unknown to us? Is the subject we are treating not of this order?

If we wish to believe that God wants to *dissolve* an **intelligent Substance**, and *strip it* of all **Faculties** of thinking and willing as soon as it *ceases to animate* a **Body**, we have no more reason for it than to believe that God wants to *overthrow* the marvelous **Order** He has established in the **Universe**, to *strip* an infinite number of **Bodies** of the *useful Qualities* He had granted them, and to *disrupt*, by this means, all of **Nature**.

Although no one can demonstrate that God *does not want* to do so, there is nevertheless no one who believes that He *wants* to do it, nor even anyone who takes the trouble to examine whether He *wants* to, or *not*. In all these respects, we are in a state of perfect **tranquility**.

<summary>The author argues that while God has the absolute power to destroy the soul, there is no evidence or rational reason to believe He intends to do so, as it would contradict the stable order observed in the rest of nature.</summary>

# SUPPLEMENT.

### FOURTEENTH SECTION

I do not claim that many people who indulge in these views cannot be individuals of integrity, possess virtue, and even make themselves very useful to humanity in the various roles they occupy. May they allow me, however, to believe that their merit is not at all the fruit of their *philosophy*, and that while being very good citizens, they may be very poor philosophers.

Moreover, in setting out here the consequences of their opinion, my aim is far less to argue against the disciples of *Spinoza* <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a Dutch philosopher whose work was often accused of promoting atheism by equating God with the natural world.</note> than to demonstrate the sole end at which the system aims. Everything within it is focused on destroying all religion in the world. Neither the love of Truth, nor the love of the public Good, nor the love of the individual Good plays any part in it. It is religion alone that they target at all costs; even if it meant plunging men into cannibalism <term>Anthropophagy: The practice of eating human flesh; the author uses this extreme term to suggest that without religion, society would descend into total savagery.</term>, it would not matter. They want no God, and in order to have none within Nature, they deify Nature itself.

I hold, therefore, to this great Principle, and nothing will make me depart from it: that *the Supreme Being, who acts upon a perfect knowledge of things, and who in his actions never deviates from the good and the just, is also most perfectly and most entirely free in all that he does.*

This will be the *specifically different weight of Bodies* <term>specifically different weight: Today we call this "density." The author is using a classic Newtonian argument: if space were entirely full of matter (a "plenum"), everything of the same size would weigh the same. ## SECTION XIX.

->*All these considerations lead us to the deepest respect, the most tender love, and the most ardent zeal for the Supreme Being.*<-

To finish these reflections with a general conclusion, let us say that a Being such as God—infinitely perfect, immense, intelligent, just, free, good, wise, and caring for His creatures—deserves our praise, our admiration, our love, our gratitude, our respect, our submission, and our trust.

Reason demands that we direct all our actions to His glory, and that we make His service the primary occupation of our lives; that we be humble and modest in the ideas we form of Him, in the discourse where His name is spoken, in the reasoning we enter into regarding His incomprehensible Essence <term>Essence: The fundamental nature of a being. The author is cautioning that while we can know God exists through reason, His actual nature remains a mystery to the human mind.</term>, and in the investigations we might conduct
